source_text: Cum ergo fidelis mater fidelis filii defuncti corpus desiderauit in basilica martyris poni, si quidem credidit eius animam meritis martyris adiuuari, hoc, quod ita credidit, supplicatio quaedam fuit, et haec profuit, si quid profuit. et quod ad idem sepulcrum recurrit animo et filium precibus magis magisque commendat, adiuuat defuncti spiritum non mortui corporis locus, sed ex loci memoria uiuus matris affectus. simul enim et quis et cui commendatus sit, non utique infructuose religiosam mentem precantis adtingit. nam et orantes de membris sui corporis faciunt quod supplicantibus congruit, cum genua figunt, cum extendunt manus uel etiam prosternuntur solo et si quid aliud faciunt uisibiliter, quamuis eorum inuisibilis uoluntas et cordis intentio deo nota sit nec ille indigeat his indiciis, ut animus ei pandatur humanus. sed hinc magis se ipsum excitat homo ad orandum gemendumque humilius atque feruentius, et nescio quomodo, cum hi motus corporis fieri nisi motu animi praecedente non possint, eisdem rursus exterius uisibiliter factis ille interior inuisibilis qui eos fecit augetur, ac per hoc cordis affectus. qui, ut fierent ista, praecessit, quia facta sunt crescit. uerum tamen si eo modo quisque teneatur uel etiam ligetur, ut haec de suis membris facere nequeat, non ideo non orat interior homo et ante oculos dei in secretissimo cubili, ubi conpungitur, sternitur. ita etiam cum plurimum intersit, ubi ponat corpus mortui sui, qui pro spiritu eius deo supplicat, quia et praecedens affectus locum elegit sanctum et illic corpore posito recordatus locus sanctus eum qui praecesserat renouat et auget affectum, tamen etiamsi non possit ubi religiosus animus elegit humare quem diligit, nullo modo debet a supplicationibus necessariis in eius commendatione cessare. ubicumque enim iaceat uel non iaceat defuncti caro, spiritui requies adquirenda est, qui cum inde exiret, secum abstulit sensum, quo interesse possit quomodo quisque sit siue in bonis siue in malis, nec ab ea carne expectat adiuuari suam uitam, cui praebebat ipse uitam, quam detraxit excedens et redditurus est rediens, quoniam non caro spiritui, sed spiritus carni etiam ipsius resurrectionis meritum comparat, utrum ad poenam an ad gloriam reuiuescat.
thought_title: A mother's prayerful affection at a martyr's shrine benefits her son's spirit
orientation: Augustine is explaining to Paulinus why a faithful mother's desire to bury her son at a martyr's basilica can benefit the dead son, not through the place itself but through the living mother's prayerful affection renewed by the place.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore when a faithful mother desired the body of her faithful dead son to be placed in the basilica of a martyr, if indeed she believed his soul to be helped by the merits of the martyr, this, which she so believed, was a kind of prayer, and this profited, if it profited anything. And because she returns in her mind to that same tomb and commends her son to prayers more and more, the place of the dead body does not help the spirit of the dead man, but from the memorial shrine of the place the living affection of the mother helps. For at the same time both who is commended and to whom he is commended touches the religious mind of the one praying not without fruit. For also those praying do with the members of their own body what is fitting for those who pray, when they bend their knees, when they stretch out their hands or even prostrate themselves on the ground and if they do anything else visibly, although their invisible will and the intention of their heart is known to God and he does not need these signs, so that the human mind may be opened to him. But from this a person rouses himself more to pray and to groan more humbly and more fervently, and I do not know how, since these movements of the body cannot happen unless a movement of the mind precedes them, by those same things being done again outwardly and visibly, that inner invisible one which made them is increased, and through this the affection of the heart, which preceded so that those things might happen, grows because they have happened. But nevertheless if anyone is held or even bound in such a way that he cannot do these things with his members, the inner man does not therefore fail to pray and prostrates himself before the eyes of God in the most secret chamber, where he is pricked. So also although it matters very much where a person places the body of his dead one, who prays to God for his spirit, because both the preceding affection chose a holy place and, the body having been placed there, the remembered holy place renews and increases the affection which had preceded, nevertheless even if he cannot bury the one whom he loves where his religious mind chose, he ought in no way to cease from the necessary prayers in his prayerful commending. For wherever the flesh of the dead person lies or does not lie, rest must be acquired for the spirit, which when it departed from there took with itself the sense by which it could be present to how anyone is whether in good things or in bad things, and it does not expect its life to be helped by that flesh, to which it itself was giving life, which it drew away when departing and is going to give back when returning, since not the flesh for the spirit, but the spirit for the flesh obtains the merit even of the resurrection itself, whether it revives to punishment or to glory.

choices.why: Keeps the architectural term basilica and the singular martyr, matching the source's focus on a martyr's shrine.
Renders quaedam as 'a kind of' to preserve the qualifying force, and supplicatio as 'prayer' per the glossary.

choices.term: ex loci memoria uiuus matris affectus
choices.english: from the memorial shrine of the place the living affection of the mother
choices.why: Uses the glossary rendering 'memorial shrine' for memoria and keeps the word order to show the contrast between the dead body's place and the living affection.
rejected: from the memory of the place
from the memorial of the place

choices.term: in secretissimo cubili, ubi conpungitur, sternitur
choices.english: prostrates himself before the eyes of God in the most secret chamber, where he is pricked
choices.why: Keeps the passive conpungitur as 'is pricked' to preserve the sense of compunction, and sternitur as 'prostrates himself' to match the earlier bodily prostration.
rejected: lies down in the most secret bedchamber, where he is moved
casts himself down in the innermost room, where he is struck

choices.why: Uses the glossary rendering 'prayerful commending' for commendatio, preserving the technical sense of commending the dead to God.

choices.term: utrum ad poenam an ad gloriam reuiuescat
choices.english: whether it revives to punishment or to glory
choices.why: Keeps the indirect question with 'whether...or' and the subjunctive force of reuiuescat as 'revives', matching the resurrection context.
rejected: whether it will revive to punishment or to glory
whether to punishment or to glory it comes back to life

pass_b_english: So when a faithful mother desired the body of her faithful deceased son to be placed in the basilica of a martyr, if she believed that his soul was helped by the merits of the martyr, that very belief was a kind of prayer, and it profited him if anything did. And when she returns in her mind to that same tomb and commends her son to God in prayer more and more, what helps the dead man's spirit is not the place of the dead body, but the living affection of the mother stirred by the memorial shrine of the place. For at the same time both who is being commended and to whom he is commended touches the devout mind of the one praying, and not without fruit. Those who pray also do with the members of their own body what suits those who entreat, when they bend their knees, when they stretch out their hands, or even prostrate themselves on the ground, and whatever else they do visibly—although their invisible will and the intention of the heart is known to God, and he does not need these signs for the human mind to be opened to him. But by these things a person stirs himself up to pray and groan more humbly and more fervently, and somehow, since these movements of the body cannot happen unless a movement of the soul precedes them, when they are done outwardly and visibly, that inner invisible movement which produced them is increased in turn, and through this the affection of the heart which preceded them grows because they were done. Yet if someone is held or even bound in such a way that he cannot do these things with his limbs, the inner man does not therefore fail to pray and prostrate himself before the eyes of God in the most secret chamber, where he is pricked. So too, although it matters greatly where a person places the body of his dead, when he prays to God for the dead man's spirit—because the affection that came first chose a holy place, and once the body is placed there, the holy place recalls and renews and increases that prior affection—nevertheless, even if he cannot bury the one he loves where his devout mind chose, he must in no way cease from the necessary prayers in his prayerful commending. For wherever the flesh of the dead lies or does not lie, rest must be obtained for the spirit, which when it departed from there took with it the sense by which it could be aware of how anyone fares, whether in good things or in evil, and it does not expect its life to be helped by that flesh to which it itself gave life, which it withdrew when it departed and will restore when it returns. For it is not the flesh that obtains for the spirit, but the spirit that obtains for the flesh even the merit of the resurrection itself, whether it revives to punishment or to glory.

last_rejected.quote: what suits those who entreat, when they bend their knees
last_rejected.source_quote: quod supplicantibus congruit, cum genua figunt
last_rejected.why: Source has 'genua figunt' (bend the knees); English omits the object 'knees'.
last_rejected.fix: what suits those who entreat, when they bend their knees
last_rejected.ruling: 'bend their knees' includes 'knees' as object; 'genua figunt' literally 'fix knees'—same meaning, no omission.

last_rejected.why: "conpungitur" means "is pricked" in the sense of being moved to compunction/repentance, not physically pricked. "Pricked" alone is ambiguous and misleading.
last_rejected.fix: where he is moved to compunction
last_rejected.ruling: "conpungitur" means compunction; "pricked" is a standard archaic rendering of compungere. Not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: For it is not the flesh that obtains for the spirit, but the spirit that obtains for the flesh even the merit of the resurrection itself
last_rejected.source_quote: non caro spiritui, sed spiritus carni etiam ipsius resurrectionis meritum comparat
last_rejected.why: "comparat" means "procures/obtains for," but the English "obtains for" is awkward and potentially reversible; more critically, "meritum" here means "reward/desert" not "merit" in the theological sense of earning. The spirit procures the resurrection reward for the flesh.
last_rejected.fix: For it is not the flesh that procures for the spirit, but the spirit that procures for the flesh even the very reward of resurrection
last_rejected.ruling: "obtains for" correctly renders "comparat"; "merit" can mean reward/desert. No meaning changed or lost.
